Val Germanasca
val jer-ma-nas'ka
n. (the highest and most isolated of the three Waldensian valleys of Piedmont, with Prali at its head)
Italian Val Germanasca, the valley of the Germanasca torrent, from a pre-Roman root; the French works call it the Val Saint-Martin.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Val Germanasca is the uppermost of the three Waldensian valleys, a narrow trench of the Cottian Alps opening from the Chisone above Perosa and climbing to Prali under the watershed, with the hamlets of Massello, Rodoretto and Salza on its flanks. It was the poorest and the least accessible of the three, which made it the last refuge in every persecution and the hardest ground for a church to serve: its congregations lay hours apart on footpaths that were shut by snow for months, its pastors travelled on foot between them, and its people lived by rye, chestnuts, goats and the talc quarries. In the great persecutions the valley was the place the others fled to, and in the expulsion of 1686 it was cleared like the rest. The dictionary enters it because the ministry of such a valley is the plainest possible test of what a pastor is for. There was no society to be gained, no stipend worth the name, and no prospect of advancement; what there was to do was to walk up a mountain in winter to preach to forty people and to catechise their children. A church which cannot staff a place like the Val Germanasca will not hold the places that are easier either, because the men who will not go there are the men who went into the ministry for something else.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a hamlet as a small village; to catechise as to instruct by question and answer; and a stipend as settled pay for services.

expand to see more

HAMLET, n. [Sax. ham, a house.] A small village; a little cluster of houses in the country.

CATECHISE, v.t. [Gr. to instruct by word of mouth.] To instruct by asking questions and correcting the answers; to question as to religious belief.

STIPEND, n. [L. stipendium.] Settled pay or compensation for services, whether daily or monthly wages or an annual salary.

ISOLATED, adj. [It. isolato.] Standing detached from others of a like kind; placed by itself; separated.

FOOTPATH, n. A narrow path or way for foot passengers only.

Key Scripture

1Pe 5:2 — "Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;"

Mat 9:37 — "Then saith he unto his disciples, The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few;"

2Ti 4:2 — "Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine."

Heb 11:38 — "(Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth."

Modern Corruption

The highest and poorest Waldensian valley, the last refuge in every persecution, whose congregations lay hours apart on footpaths shut by snow.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live corruption is the career ministry: men entering the pastorate as a profession with a ladder in it, so that the small, cold, distant and poor congregations are staffed by whoever could not get anything better, and are understood by everybody to be a stage. The apostolic requirement is the opposite and is stated without any allowance: “not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind” (1Pe 5:2). A valley like this exposes the motive because it offers nothing else.

The principle to recover is the sufficiency of the charge itself. “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2) is the whole of the commission, and it says nothing about the size of the congregation. The dictionary holds that the health of a church may be measured fairly accurately by how its smallest and most inconvenient congregations are served, and that this is a measurement most denominations avoid taking.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek poimaino (G4165), to tend a flock; Greek ergates (G2040), a workman, a field labourer.

expand to see more

Greek poimaino (G4165) — to tend, to shepherd a flock; “Feed the flock of God which is among you”, 1 Peter 5:2.

Greek aischrokerdos (G147) — for base gain; “not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind”, 1 Peter 5:2.

Greek ergates (G2040) — a workman, a labourer; “but the labourers are few”, Matthew 9:37.

Greek kerusso (G2784) — to proclaim as a herald; “Preach the word”, 2 Timothy 4:2.

Greek oros (G3735) — a mountain; “they wandered in deserts, and in mountains”, Hebrews 11:38.

Usage

"“Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof” (1Pe 5:2) — congregations hours apart on footpaths shut by snow."

"“The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few” (Mat 9:37) — the poorest of the three valleys, and the last refuge."

"“Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2) — forty people up a mountain in winter."
